units.translation: 485. And she laughed: this too is a sign of frivolity, since Isocrates (Ad Demon. 15) says: 'Do not cherish precipitate laughter'.
486a. With mocking words: with ironic words, able to cut and pain the heart. And 'winking' means mocking with the eyes; for 'squint-eyed' people are called 'epilloi'.

487-89a. Come now: through both he mocks Idmon, first as an unskilled seer, and second as one who takes pride in Apollo his father as being very powerful to bring down the arrogant. And he does this with a threat, reviling him.
491a. The word 'chreio' indicates both what is said according to need and fate, and what is destined. P

c. Prophesying a vain chreio: worthy of regret. It is also written 'metamonion', which means vain, carried away with the winds. From a plural genitive a possessive form in -ios is made, with iota in the penultimate syllable, as 'allon' 'allonios', 'anemon' 'anemonios'.
492. He was angry, rebuking: he was enraged and angered, speaking ill and blaming.

494-95. With the left hand: by euphemism, with the left hand. 'He tested' instead of 'he fitted'. The 'ana' is redundant; for the sequence is: 'and Orpheus'. Unless, indeed, from the 'ana' he means 'having stood up': 'and Orpheus having stood up'. He does this in order to put an end to the factions and rivalries by his own music.

496-98a. He sang how the earth: he wishes to sing of the first confusion of the elements, how from some strife each obtained its own place and took its order. The song is also appropriate to the present circumstances, because it is fitting to cease from battle and return to one's proper disposition.

b. From destructive strife: Empedocles (cf. 31 B 17 sqq. Diels-Kranz) says that when all things were previously mixed together, strife and love, being introduced, brought about the separation, and apart from these nothing...
